##### **By Faatimah Majothi**

![](https://www.classicescapes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/Kentucky-Derby.CQ_-e1525419167940.jpg)

In the United Kingdom, sports are a big part of the entertainment industry. Football is famously one of the most popular sports thanks to championships and leagues featuring teams from many major towns and cities across the country. 
Watching and attending games, betting on scores and keeping track of favourite teams and players are familiar activities to many, if not most British people. As a result, betting companies have many branches in most cities, towns, and even villages across the country.

The royal family is also a topic of great interest across the nation. Queen Elizabeth II was arguably the most iconic British royal in the country, and was very popular during her reign until her death in 2022. After her death on the 9th of September in 2022, the national news outlets were flooded with information relating to her, and a mourning period of ten days was announced.

In this project we will be taking a look at how the Queen's death and consequential national mourning period affected the British public.

We will look at three of the most popular sports:

- Football

- Tennis

- Horse races


We will then go on to investigate the effects of the event on the stock prices of some of the betting companies that have a big presence in the United Kingdom. The three betting company stocks we will investigate are not based in the UK, but have many branches and a strong footing in the country. 

The stocks we have selected are:

- [FLUT] Flutter Entertainment plc (Owns Betfair and PaddyPower, both common in Britain)

- [CZR] Caesars Entertainment Inc (Owns William Hill, previously Britain's leading betting company)

- [ENT.L] Entain PLC (Owns Ladbrokes and Coral, both common in Britain)


### The Data:

##### Setup:
```{r}
# Import libraries
library(gtrendsR)
library(quantmod)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyverse)
library(maps)
install.packages('corrplot')
library(corrplot)
library(lubridate)

# Save current warn option to restore later
old_warn_option <- getOption('warn')

# Suppress all warnings
options(warn = -1)

# Get stock symbols for the four companies
getSymbols(c('FLUT', 'CZR', 'ENT.L'))
```


### The Stock Data:

To begin with, we create a dataframe containing the closing prices of the stocks we selected.
```{r}
# Create individual data frames for each stock
flut_df <- data.frame(Date = as.Date(row.names(as.data.frame(FLUT))), Close1 = FLUT$FLUT.Close)
czr_df <- data.frame(Date = as.Date(row.names(as.data.frame(CZR))), Close2 = CZR$CZR.Close)
ent_df <- data.frame(Date = as.Date(row.names(as.data.frame(ENT.L))), Close3 = ENT.L$ENT.L.Close)

# Merge all data frames by Date
all_stocks <- list(flut_df, czr_df, ent_df) %>%
  reduce(full_join, by = 'Date')

# Reshape for plotting
long_stocks <- all_stocks %>%
  pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = 'Stock', values_to = 'Close')
```
We can then look at the closing prices of the stocks we have selected. The graph below shows the prices for the stocks between 2020 to 2025.
```{r}
# Filter dates and visualise
long_stocks %>%
  filter(Date >= as.Date('2015-01-01') & Date <= as.Date('2025-12-31')) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = Date, y = Close, color = Stock)) +
  scale_color_discrete(name = 'Company', labels = c('Flutter Ent.', 'Caesars Ent.', 'Entain PLC')) +
  labs(title = 'Stock Prices of Streaming Services', y = 'Stock Price')
```
We can "zoom in" on this graph to take a closer look at the years 2021-2023.

```{r}
# Visualise data for 2021-2023
long_stocks %>%
  filter(Date >= '2021-01-01' & Date <= '2023-12-31') %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = Date, y = Close, color = Stock)) +
  scale_color_discrete(name = 'Company', labels = c('Flutter Ent.', 'Caesars Ent.', 'Entain PLC')) +
  labs(title = 'Stock Prices of Streaming Services (2021-2023)', y = 'Stock Price')

```
Both graphs display the relatively **higher volatility** of Caesars Entertainment stocks. This was perhaps due to higher stock prices and popularity at the time. Deeper research revealed that the three companies have different areas of focus. Flutter Ent. is an **online betting** company, while Entain PLC is a **sports-betting and gaming** company. Caesars Ent. differs in that it operates as a **gaming and hospitality** company in the United States aside from betting.
We can infer from this that Caesars Ent. has higher volatility as well as stock prices because of its non-sports or betting related earnings.
Their ownership of William Hill and their provision of online betting services are the reason for their inclusion as a stock in this analysis.

##### **Sources**: [StockAnalysis (Entain)]('https://stockanalysis.com/quote/lon/ENT/'), [StockInvest (Caesars)]('https://stockinvest.us/info/CZR'), [Flutter]('https://flutter.com/')


### The Trend Data:

##### Setup:
```{r}
# Create DataFrame of gtrends
uk_sports <-  gtrends(keyword=c('football', 'tennis', 'horse racing'), geo = 'GB', time = '2021-01-01 2023-12-31')
```

To begin exploring the Google Trends data, we first import the search data for our chosen sport into the `uk_sports` DataFrame. We can then begin exploring the data available through visualisation.

```{r}
# Remove missing values
trends_over_time <- uk_sports$interest_over_time %>% replace_na(list(hits = 0))

# Visualise
trends_over_time %>% ggplot() + geom_line(aes(date, hits, color = keyword)) +
  scale_color_discrete(name = 'Sport', labels = c('Football','Tennis','Horse Races' )) + 
  labs(title = 'Google Trend Data For Sports', y = 'Hits (Normalized to be between 0 and 1000
       ', x = 'Date', subtitle = 'Sports search trends in the United Kingdom')
```
Immediately, we notice a pattern in the Google search trends for `Horse Races` and `Football`. Both sports appear to have significant spikes of interest or disinterest **around the middle months** of each year displayed on the graph.To understand these patterns, we will have to investigate further.

Through basic external research, we can associate the **peaks of interest in horse racing** with the major UK horse racing festivals, such as the Royal Ascot and the Cheltenham Festival, which run annually around the April-June period. 

Similarly, the UK Premier League football tournament (which runs annually around the August-May period) **coincides with the spikes** in search trend data around the middle of the years featured on our graph. The highest peak of interest in football in the UK coincides with the September of 2022. This is a notable point for further investigation, as the Queen's death occurred around that time period. It is worth noting that there is a **plunge in hits** just before this peak of interest. 

Lastly, the search hits for `Tennis` have few significant peaks and troughs in the trend graph. There appears to be a pattern of very small peaks in the first quarter of each year, which according to external research, can be linked with the British tennis season during which multiple major tennis events are held. 

###### **Sources:**
- ([Horse racing calendar UK]('https://horseracewinner.com/uk-racing-calendar/'))
- ([Football Premier League UK]('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_League'))
- ([Tennis Season UK]('https://www.countryandtownhouse.com/culture/british-tennis-season/'))

Keeping this overview of the trends over the years before and after the Queen's death in mind, we can now zoom in on the search trend data closer to the time of her death in September 2022. For ease of visibility, we will zoom in on the 9th of September and the 30 days before and after.

```{r}
# Filter dates
zoomed_trends <- uk_sports$interest_over_time  %>% replace_na(list(hits = 0)) %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date('2022-08-10') & date <= as.Date('2022-10-09'))

# Visualise labelled trend graph
max_points <- zoomed_trends %>%
  group_by(keyword) %>%
  slice_max(hits, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

min_points <- zoomed_trends %>%
  group_by(keyword) %>%
  slice_min(hits, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

zoomed_trends %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, hits, color = keyword)) +
  geom_text(data = max_points, aes(date, hits, label = date), vjust = -0.25, hjust = -0.1) +
  geom_point(data = max_points, aes(date, hits), color = 'black', size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = min_points, aes(date, hits, label = date), vjust = -1, hjust = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = min_points, aes(date, hits), color = 'black', size = 2) +
  labs(title = 'Google Trend Data For Sports', y = 'Hits (Normalized to be between 0 and 1000
       ', x = 'Date', subtitle = 'Gtrend hits for sports in the UK around Queen Elizabeth II\'s death')
```
We can now see that both horse racing and football had a decrease in hits around the time of Queen Elizabeth II's death, though interest in tennis **did not show any significant change**. However, we **cannot yet determine** whether the Queen's death was the sole cause for the drop in interest in the two sports.
The previous graph also displayed significant fluctuation in hits for `football` prior to the Queen's passing, which is likely due to the immense popularity of the sport combined with the lower frequency of regular events.

### Correlations

Our next step is to investigate the **correlations** between the betting stocks and `gtrends` data. To do this, we will perform some data cleaning and merging before plotting a correlation matrix.
```{r}
# Clean Dataframes for merge
select_stocks <- select_stocks %>% replace_na(list(hits = 0)) %>% rename(date = Date)

head(select_stocks)
```
```{r}
# Clean Dataframes for merge
gg_trends <- trends_over_time %>% replace_na(list(hits = 0)) %>% mutate(date = as.Date(date)) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = 'keyword', 
values_from = 'hits')
gg_trends <- gg_trends %>% mutate(week = floor_date(date, 'week', week_start = 2)) %>% group_by(week) %>% summarize(across(where(is.numeric), mean)) %>% rename(date = week)

head(gg_trends)
```
```{r}
# Join DataFrames
stocks_hits <- inner_join(gg_trends, select_stocks, by = 'date')

head(stocks_hits)
```
```{r}
# Display correlations
cor_matrix <- cor(select(stocks_hits, FLUT.Close, CZR.Close, ENT.L.Close, football, tennis, `horse racing`), use = 'complete.obs')

corrplot(cor_matrix, method = 'color')
```
When making observations based on the correlation matrix, we will keep in mind two things: the strength and direction of correlations **between the three stocks**, and the strength and direction of the correlations **between each stock and sport**. We will ignore the dark **diagonal values**, as they do not provide us with information.

Stocks:

- None of the stocks have negative correlations (stocks do not tend to move in opposite directions).
- `ENT.L` has a **weak positive correlation** of around 0.2 with `FLUT`. It has a stronger positive correlation with `CZR` (0.8 approx.), indicating that `ENT.L` stocks tend to **move in the same direction** as `CZR` stocks.
- `CZR` has a weaker positive correlation with `FLUT` (0.3-0.4 approx.) than with `ENT.L` (0.8 approx.). We can infer from this that `CZR` stock prices are **somewhat likely to move in the same direction** as `FLUT` stocks.
- `FLUT` having the weakest positive correlations to other stocks may be due to the **different nature of stocks held** by Flutter Ent. in comparison to Entain PLC and Caesars Ent. stocks, as Flutter primarily focuses on online betting apps.

Stocks and Trends:

- `ENT.L` stock prices appear to have **little to no correlation** with `football` search hits in the UK. However, there appears to be some **weak positive correlation** (around 0.1) between the company's stocks and `tennis` and `horse racing` hits.
- `CZR` stock prices do not appear to have significant correlation with the search hits of the three sports (at least in the UK). The graph shows a very **faint positive correlation** with `football` (below 0.1). We can therefore consider the fact that Caesars Ent., being based mainly in America, may be influenced **less by the more local sports** (UK `tennis` and `horse racing`) and more by the **internationally popular** `football` leagues.
- Curiously, `FLUT` stock prices appear to **correlate negatively** with `horse racing` search hits in the UK, though weakly so (below 0.2). `football` search hits have a **weak positive correlation** with `FLUT` stock prices, while `tennis` search hits in the UK **do not** appear to have any correlation with the company's stocks at all. 

##### **NOTE: During this project's investigation, we did not find any explanation for the inverse correlation between `FLUT` stocks and horse racing. This can be considered a limitation of our investigation.**


### Combining Data

We now have a basic view of the distributions and correlations of the stock and trend data. With this overview in mind, we can begin to combine and compare the `gtrends` and stock data for further analysis. We will plot both DataFrames against each other and take a closer look at the patterns between stocks and hits around the date of the Queen's death in September 2022.
```{r}
# Filtering data by date
select_stocks <- all_stocks %>% filter(Date >= '2021-01-01' & Date <= '2023-12-31')

# Map stock names
stock_cols <- c('FLUT.Close', 'CZR.Close', 'ENT.L.Close')
stock_labels <- c('Flutter Ent.', 'Caesars Ent.', 'Entain PLC')

for (i in seq_along(stock_cols)) {
  stock_col <- stock_cols[i]
  stock_label <- stock_labels[i]
  
  # Plot
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = select_stocks, aes_string(x = 'Date', y = stock_col), color = 'black', linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_line(data = trends_over_time, aes(x = date, y = hits * 10, color = keyword)) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = paste0(stock_label, ' Stock Price'),
      sec.axis = sec_axis(~./10, name = 'Google Trends Hits')
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste0(stock_label, ' Stock Price vs Sports Google Trends'),
      color = 'Sport'
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date('2022-09-08'), linetype = 'dashed', color = 'red') +
  annotate('text', x = as.Date('2022-09-08'), y = Inf, label = 'Queen Elizabeth II\'s Death', vjust = 2, hjust = -0.05, color = 'red')
  print(p)
}
```
```{r}
# Filter and plot zoomed stocks
filter_stocks <- all_stocks %>% filter(Date >= '2022-08-10' & Date <= '2022-10-09')
filter_trends <- trends_over_time %>% filter(date >= '2022-08-10' & date <= '2022-10-09')

for (i in seq_along(stock_cols)) {
  stock_col <- stock_cols[i]
  stock_label <- stock_labels[i]
  
  # Plot
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = filter_stocks, aes_string(x = 'Date', y = stock_col), color = 'black', linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_line(data = filter_trends, aes(x = date, y = hits * 10, color = keyword)) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = paste0(stock_label, ' Stock Price'),
      sec.axis = sec_axis(~./10, name = 'Google Trends Hits')
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste0(stock_label, ' Stock Price vs Sports Google Trends'),
      color = 'Sport'
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date('2022-09-08'), linetype = 'dashed', color = 'red') +
  annotate('text', x = as.Date('2022-09-08'), y = Inf, label = 'Queen Elizabeth II\'s Death', vjust = 2, hjust = -0.05, color = 'red')
  print(p)
}

```
With our betting company stocks plotted against the `gtrends` data, we can make the following observations:

- **Flutter Ent:** There is **no apparent correlation** between the general trend data for `tennis` and `horse racing` and Flutter Ent's closing stock prices over the time period. However, there seems to be a drop in stock prices after the Queen's death which **correlates** with the drop in `football` search hits in the UK after that 8th.
- **Caesars Ent:** There is **no apparent correlation** between the general trend data for `tennis` and `horse racing` and Caesars Ent's closing stock prices over the time period. Similarly to the previous graph, there does appear to be some **minor correlation** 
between the drop in `football` search hits in the UK and the small drop in Caesars Ent stocks after the Queen's death.
- **Entain PLC:** Unlike the others, Entain PLC's stocks appear to have experienced an increase in stock prices around the time of the Queen's death. There appears to be a general **correlation** between `football` hits and stock prices. Additionally, there seems to be a **weak inverse correlation** between interest in `football` and Entain PLC stocks after the Queen's passing on September 8th. There **does not appear to be any correlation** between hits for the other two sports and the company's stock prices around that time.
